div.head:
[B1]
M. William Shak-speare (qq2)
HIS
Historie, of King Lear.
Actus Primus. Scœna Prima.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
I thought the King had more affected the
Duke of Albany then Cornwell.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
It did allwaies seeme so to vs, but
now in the diuision of the kingdomes, it ap­
peares not which of the Dukes he values
most, for equalities are so weighed, that curiositie in nei­
ther, can make choise of eithers moytie.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Is not this your sonne my Lord?

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
His breeding sir hath beene at my charge, I haue
so often blusht to acknowledge him, that now I am
braz’d to it.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I cannot conceiue you.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
Sir, this young fellowes mother Could, wher­
upon shee grew round wombed, and had indeed Sir a
sonne for her cradle, ere she had a husband for her bed,
doe you smell a fault?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
I cannot wish the fault vndone, the issue of it
being so proper.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
But I haue sir a sonne by order of Law, some
yeare elder then this, who yet is no deerer in my ac­
count, though this knaue came something sawcely into the
world before hee was sent for, yet was his mother faire,
there was good sport at his makeing, & the whoreson must
be acknowledged, do you know this noble gentle­
man Edmund?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: No my Lord.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
My Lord of Kent,
remember him hereafter as my honorable friend.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: My seruices to your Lordship.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I must loue you, and sue to know you better.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Sir I shall study deseruing.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
Hee hath beene out nine yeares, and away hee shall
againe, the King is comming.

div.stage:
Sound a Sennet. Enter one bearing a Coronet, then Lear, then the
Dukes of Albany, and Cornwell, next Gonorill, Re­
gan, Cordelia, with followers.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Attend my Lords of France and Burgundy, Gloster.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: I shall my Leige.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Meane time we will expresse our darker purposes,
The map there; know we haue diuided
In three, our kingdome; and tis our first intent,
To shake all cares and busines of our state,
Confirming them on yonger yeares, while we
Vnburthen’d crawle toward death. Our son of Cornwal,
And you our no lesse louing Sonne of Albany, (qq2b)
We haue this houre a constant will to publish
Our daughters seuerall Dowers, that future strife
May be preuented now. The two great Princes France and Burgundy,
Great ryuals in our youngest daughters loue,
Long in our Court haue made their amorous soiourne,
And here are to be answerd, tell me my daughters,
(Since now we will diuest vs both of Rule,
Interest of Territory, Cares of State)
Which of you shall we say doth loue vs most,
That we our largest bountie may extend,
Where merit doth most challenge it,
Gonorill our eldest borne, speake first?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Sir I do loue you more then words can weild the matter,
Dearer then eye-sight, space or libertie,
Beyond what can be valued rich or rare,
No lesse then life; with grace, health, beautie, honour,
As much a child ere loued, or father friend,
A loue that makes breath poore, and speech vnable,
Beyond all manner of so much I loue you.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: What shall Cordelia doe, loue and be silent.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Of al these bounds, euen from this line to this,
With shady forrests, and with Champains rich’d
With plenteous Riuers, and wide skirted meades,
We make thee Lady, to thine and Albaines issue,
Be this perpetuall, what saies our second daughter? [B2]
Our deerest Regan, wife to Cornwell, speake?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
Sir I am made of the selfe same mettall that my sister is,
And prize me at her worth in my true heart,
I find she names my very deed of loue, onely she came short,
That I professe my selfe an enemie to all other ioyes,
Which the most precious square of sence possesses,
And find I am alone felicitate, in your deere highnes loue.

p.nvsSeg: & yet not so, since I am sure

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
To thee and thine hereditarie euer
Remaine this ample third of our faire kingdome,
No lesse in space, validity, and pleasure,
Then that confirm’d on Gonorill, but now our ioy,
Although the last, not least in our deere loue,
The Vines of France, and Milke of Burgundie,
Striue to be interest.
What can you say to win a third, more opulent
Then your sisters. speake.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p: Nothing my Lord.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Nothing?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: How, nothing can come of nothing, speake againe.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p:
Vnhappie that I am, I cannot heaue
my heart into my mouth, I loue your Maiestie
according to my bond, nor more nor lesse.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Goe to, goe to, mend your speech a little,
Least it may mar your fortunes.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p:
Good my Lord,
You haue begot me, bred me, loued me,
I returne those duties backe as are right fit,
Obey you, loue you, and most honour you,
Why haue my sisters husbands if they say they loue you all,
Happely when I shall wed, that Lord whose hand
Must take my plight, shall cary halfe my loue with him,
Halfe my care and duty, sure I shall neuer
Mary like my sisters, to loue my father all.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: But goes this with thy heart?

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p: I good my Lord.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: So yong and so vntender.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p: So yong my Lord and true.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Well let it be so, thy truth then be thy dower,
For by the sacred radience of the Sunne, [B2v]
The mistresse of Heccat, and the might,
By all the operation of the orbs,
From whome we doe exsist and cease to be
Heere I disclaime all my paternall care,
Propinquitie and property of blood,
And as a stranger to my heart and me
Hould thee from this for euer, the barbarous Scythyan,
Or he that makes his generation
Messes to gorge his appetite
Shall to my bosome bee as well neighbour’d, pittyed and relieued
As thou my sometime daughter.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Good my Liege.

Peace Kent, come not between the Dragon & his wrath,
I lou’d her most, and thought to set my rest
On her kind nurcery, hence and auoide my sight?
So be my graue my peace as here I giue,
Her fathers heart from her, call France, who stirres?
Call Burgundy, Cornwell, and Albany,
With my two daughters dower digest this third,
Let pride, which she cals plainnes, marrie her:
I doe inuest you iointly in my powre,
Preheminence, and all the large effects
That troope with Maiestie, our selfe by monthly course
With reseruation of an hundred knights,
By you to be sustayn’d, shall our abode
Make with you by due turnes, onely we still retaine
The name and all the additions to a King,
The sway, reuenue, execution of the rest,
Beloued sonnes be yours, which to confirme,
This Coronet part betwixt you.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Royall Lear,
Whom I haue euer honor’d as my King,
Loued as my Father, as my maister followed,
As my great patron thought on in my prayers.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: The bow is bẽt & drawen make from the shaft,

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Let it fall rather,
Though the forke inuade the region of my heart,
Be Kent vnmannerly when Lear is man, [B3]
What wilt thou doe ould man, think’st thou that dutie
Shall haue dread to speake, when power to flatterie bowes,
To plainnes honours bound when Maiestie stoops to folly,
Reuerse thy doome, and in thy best consideration (qq2vb)
Checke this hideous rashnes, answere my life
My iudgement, thy yongest daughter does not loue thee least,
Nor are those empty harted whose low, sound
Reuerbs no hollownes.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Kent on thy life no more.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
My life I neuer held but as a pawne
To wage against thy enemies, nor feare to lose it
Thy safty being the motiue.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Out of my sight.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
See better Lear and let me still remaine,
The true blanke of thine eye.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Now by Appollo,

p.nvsSeg: thou swearest thy Gods in vaine.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Vassall, recreant.

sp.speaker: Alb. Cor.
sp.p: Deare Sir forbeare.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Doe, kill thy Physicion,
And the fee bestow vpon the foule disease,
Reuoke thy doome, or whilst I can vent clamour
From my throat, ile tell thee thou dost euill.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Heare me recreant, on thy allegeance heare me?
Since thou hast sought to make vs breake our vow,
Which we durst neuer yet; and with straied pride,
To come betweene our sentence and our powre,
Which nor our nature nor our place can beare,
Our potency made good, take thy reward,
Foure dayes we doe allot thee for prouision,
To shield thee from diseases of the world,
And on the fift to turne thy hated backe
Vpon our kingdome, if on the tenth day following,
Thy banisht truncke be found in our dominions,
The moment is thy death, away, by Iupiter
This shall not be reuokt.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Why fare thee well king, since thus thou wilt appeare,
Friendship liues hence, and banishment is here,
The Gods to their protection take the maide, [B3v]
That rightly thinks, and hast most iustly said,
And your large speeches may your deedes approue,
That good effects may spring from wordes of loue:
Thus Kent O Princes, bids you all adew,
Heele shape his old course in a countrie new.

div.stage: Enter France and Burgundie with Gloster.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Heers France and Burgundie my noble Lord.

p.nvsSeg: or cease your quest of loue?
I craue no more then what

sp.p:
Right noble Burgundie, when she was deere to vs
We did hold her so, but now her prise is fallen,
Sir there she stands, if ought within that little
Seeming substãce, or al of it with our displeasure peec’st,
And nothing else may fitly like your grace,
Shees there, and she is yours.

sp.speaker: Burg.
sp.p: I know no answer.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Sir will you with those infirmities she owes,
Vnfriended, new adopted to our hate,
Couered with our curse, and stranger’d with our oth,
Take her or leaue her.

Pardon me royall sir, election makes not vp
On such conditions.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Then leaue her sir, for by the powre that made me
I tell you all her wealth, for you great King,
I would not from your loue make such a stray,
To match you where I hate, therefore beseech you,
To auert your liking a more worthier way,
Then on a wretch whome nature is ashamed
Almost to acknowledge hers.

This is most strange, that she, that euen but now
Was your best obiect, the argument of your praise,
Balme of your age, most best, most deerest,
Should in this trice of time commit a thing,
So monstrous to dismantell so many foulds of fauour, [B4]
Sure her offence must be of such vnnaturall degree,
That monsters it, or you for voucht affections
Falne into taint, which to beleeue of her
Must be a faith that reason without miracle
Could neuer plant in me.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p:
I yet beseech your Maiestie,
If for I want that glib and oyly Art,
To speake and purpose not, since what I well entend
Ile do’t before I speake, that you may know
It is no vicious blot, murder or foulnes,
No vncleane action or dishonord step
That hath depriu’d me of your grace and fauour,
But euen for want of that, for which I am rich,
A still soliciting eye, and such a tongue,
As I am glad I haue not, though not to haue it,
Hath lost me in your liking.

Goe to, goe to, better thou hadst not bin borne,
Then not to haue pleas’d me better.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p:
Is it no more but this, a tardines in nature,
That often leaues the historie vnspoke that it intends to do,
My Lord of Burgundie, what say you to the Lady?
Loue is not loue when it is mingled with respects that stãds
Aloofe from the intire point wil you haue her?
She is her selfe and dowre.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p: Nothing, I haue sworne. I am firme.

sp.speaker: Burg.
sp.p:
I am sory then you haue so lost a father,
That you must loose a husband.

p.nvsSeg: I shall not be his wife.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p:
Fairest Cordelia that art most rich being poore,
Most choise forsaken, and most loued despisd,
Thee and thy vertues here I ceaze vpon,
Be it lawfull I take vp whats cast away,
Gods, Gods! tis strãge, that from their couldst neglect,
My loue should kindle to inflam’d respect, [B4v]
Thy dowreles daughter King throwne to thy chance,
Is Queene of vs, of ours, and our faire France:
Not all the Dukes in watrish Burgundie,
Shall buy this vnprizd precious maide of me,
Bid them farewell Cordelia, though vnkind
Thou loosest here, a better where to find.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Thou hast her France, let her be thine,
For we haue no such daughter, nor shall euer see
That face of hers againe, therfore be gone, (qq3b)
Without our grace, our loue, our benizon? come noble Burgũdy.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Bid farewell to your sisters?

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p:
The iewels of our father,
With washt eyes Cordelia leaues you, I know you what you are,
And like a sister am most loath to call your faults
As they are named, vse well our Father,
To your professed bosoms I commit him,
But yet alas stood I within his grace,
I would preferre him to a better place:
So farewell to you both?

sp.speaker: Gonorill.
sp.p: Prescribe not vs our duties?

div.sp:
Regan.Let your study be to content your Lord,
Who hath receaued you at Fortunes almes,
You haue obedience scanted,
And well are worth the worth that you haue wanted.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p:
Time shal vnfould what pleated cũning hides,
Who couers faults, at last shame them derides:
Well may you prosper.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Come faire Cordelia?

sp.speaker: Gonor.
sp.p:
Sister, it is not a little I haue to say,
Of what most neerely appertaines to vs both,
I thinke our father will hence to night.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: Thats most certaine, and with you, next moneth with vs.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
You see how full of changes his age is, the ob­
seruation we haue made of it hath not bin little; hee alwaies
loued our sister most, and with what poore iudgement hee
hath now cast her off, appeares too grosse.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
Tis the infirmitie of his age, yet hee hath euer but [C1]
slenderly knowne himselfe.

sp.speaker: Gono.
sp.p:
The best and soundest of his time hath bin but
rash, then must we looke to receiue from his age not a­
lone the imperfection of long ingrafted condition, but
therwithal vnruly waywardnes, that infirme and
cholericke yeares bring with them.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p:
Such vnconstant starts are we like to haue from
him, as this of Kents banishment.

sp.speaker: Gono.
sp.p:
There is further complement of leaue taking be­
tweene France and him, pray lets hit together, if our
Father cary authority with such dispositions as he beares,
this last surrender of his, will but offend vs,

sp.speaker: Ragan.
sp.p: We shall further thinke on’t.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: We must doe something, and it’h heate.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
Thou Nature art my Goddesse, to thy law
my seruices are bound, wherefore should I
stand in the plague of custome, and permit
the curiositie of nations to depriue me,
for that I am some twelue or 14. mooneshines
lag of a brother, why bastard? wherfore base,
when my dementions are as well compact,
my mind as generous, and my shape as true
as honest madams issue, why brand they vs
with base, base bastardie? Base, Base?
who in the lusty stealth of nature, take
more composition and feirce quality,
then doth within a stale dull lyed bed,
goe to the creating of a whole tribe of fops
got tweene a sleepe and wake; well the
legitimate Edgar, I must haue your land,
our Fathers loue is to the bastard Edmund,
as to the legitimate, fine word: Legitimate. (qq3va)
well my legitimate, if this letter speede,
and my inuention thriue, Edmund the base
shall tooth’legitimate: I grow, I prosper,
now Gods stand vp for Bastards.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
Kent banisht thus, and France in choller parted,
and the King gone to night, subscribd his power,
confined to exhibition, all this donne
vpon the gadde; Edmund how now what newes?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: So please your Lordship, none.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Why so earnestly seeke you to put vp that letter?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: I know no newes my Lord.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: What paper were you reading?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Nothing my Lord,

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
No, what needes then that terrible dispatch of
it into your pocket, the qualitie of nothing hath not
such need to hide it selfe, lets see, come if it bee no­
thing I shall not neede spectacles.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.p:
I beseech you Sir pardon me, it is a letter
from my brother, that I haue not all ore read, for so
much as I haue perused, I find it not fit for your li­
king.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Giue me the letter sir.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
I shall offend either to detaine or giue it,
the contents as in part I vnderstand them,
are too blame.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Lets see, lets see?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
I hope for my brothers iustification, he wrot
this but as an essay, or tast of my vertue.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
This policie and reuerence of age makes the
world bitter to the best of our times, keepes our fortunes from
vs till our oldnes cannot relish them, I begin to find an idle
and fond bondage in the oppression of aged tyranny, who swaies
not as it hath power, but as it is suffered, come to me, that of
this I may speake more, if our father would sleepe till I wakt
him, you should inioy halfe his reuenew for euer, and liue the
beloued of your brother Edgar.
Hum, conspiracie, slept till I wakt him, you should
enioy halfe his reuenew, my sonne Edgar, had hee a
hand to write this, a hart, and braine to breed it in,
when came this to you, who brought it?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
It was not brought me my Lord, ther’s the
cunning of it, I found it throwne in at the casement of
my closet.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: You know the Caractar to be your brothers?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
If the matter were good, my Lord I durst sweare
it were his but in respect, of that I would faine thinke it
were not,

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: It is his?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
It is his hand my Lord, but I hope his heart is
not in the contents.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Hath he neuer heretofore soũded you in this busines?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
Neuer my Lord, but I haue often heard him main­
taine it to be fit, that sons at perfit age, & fathers
declining, his father should be as ward to the sonne, and
the sonne mannage the reuenew.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
O villaine, villaine, his very opinion in the let­
ter, abhorred villaine, vnnaturall detested brutish
villaine, worse then brutish, go sir seeke him, I
apprehend him, abhominable villaine where is he?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
I doe not well know my Lord, if it shall please you to
suspend your indignation against my brother, til you can
deriue from him better testimony of this intent: you should
run a certaine course, where if you violently proceed a­
gainst him, mistaking his purpose, it would make a great
gap in your owne honour, & shake in peeces the heart of (qq3vb)
his obediẽce, I dare pawn downe my life for him,
he hath wrote this to feele my affection to your honour, and
to no further pretence of danger.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Thinke you so?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
If your honour iudge it meete, I will place you
where you shall heare vs conferre of this, and by an auri­
gular assurance haue your satisfaction, and that without
any further delay then this very euening.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: He cannot be such a monster.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Nor is not sure.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
To his father, that so tenderly and intirely loues him,
heauen and earth! Edmund seeke
him out, wind mee into him, I pray you frame your bu­
sines after your own wisedome, I would vnstate my
selfe to be in a due resolution

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
I shall seeke him sir presently, conuey the bu­
sinesse as I shall see meanes, and acquaint you withall.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
These late eclipses in the Sunne and Moone por­
tend no good to vs, though the wisedome of nature can
reason thus and thus, yet nature finds it selfe scourg’d
by the sequent effects, loue cooles, friendship fals off,
brothers diuide, in Citties mutinies, in Countries dis­
cords, Pallaces treason, the bond crackt betweene
sonne and father; This villaine of mine comes vnder the
prediction; there’s Son against Father, the King fals from
byas of Nature, there’s Father against Childe. We haue
seene the best of our time. Machinations, hollownesse,
treacherie, and all ruinous disorders follow vs disquietly
to our Graues. find out this villaine Edmund, it shal loose
thee nothing, doe it carefully, and the noble and true har­
ted Kent banisht, his offence honest, strange strange!

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
This is the excellent foppery of the world, that
when we are sicke in Fortune, often the surfeit of our owne
behauiour, we make guiltie of our disasters, the Sunne, the
Moone, and the Starres, as if we were Villaines by necessitie,
Fooles by heauenly compulsion, Knaues, Theeues, and [C2v]
Trecherers by spirituall predominance, Drunkards, Ly­
ars, and Adulterers by an enforst obedience of planitary
influence, and all that wee are euill in, by a diuine thru­
sting on, an admirable euasion of whoremaster man,
to lay his gotish disposition to the charge of Starres:
my Father compounded with my Mother vnder the Dra­
gons taile, and my natiuitie was vnder Vrsa maior, so
that it followes, I am rough and lecherous, Fut, I should
haue beene that I am, had the maidenlest starre of the Fir­
mament twinckled on my bastardy.
Enter Edgar
Edgar; and out hee comes like the Catastrophe of the old Comedy,
mine is villanous melancholy, with a sith like them
of Bedlam; O these eclipses doe portend these diui­
sions. Fa, Sol, La, Me.

sp.speaker: Edgar.
sp.p:
How now brother Edmund, what serious con­
templation are you in?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
I am thinking brother of a prediction I read this
other day, what should follow these Eclipses.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Doe you busie your selfe about that?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
I promise you the effects he writ of, succeed
vnhappily, as of vnnaturalnesse betweene the child and the parent, death,
dearth, dissolutions of ancient amities, diuisions in state, mena­
ces and maledictions against King and nobles, needles diffiden­
ces, banishment of friẽds, dissipation of Cohorts, nuptial breach­
es, and I know not what.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: How long haue you beene a sectary Astronomicall?
Come, come, when saw you my father last?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Why, the night gon by.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Spake you with him?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Two houres together.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
Parted you in good tearmes? found you no dis­
pleasure in him by word or countenance?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: None at all.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
Bethinke your selfe wherein you may haue offen­
ded him, and at my intreatie, forbeare his presence, till
some little time hath qualified the heat of his displeasure,
which at this instant so rageth in him, that with the mis­ (qq4a)
chiefe, of your parson it would scarce allay.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Some villaine hath done me wrong.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
Thats my feare I pray you haue a continent
forbearance till the speed of his rage goes slower: and as
I say, retire with me to my lodging, from whence I will
fitly bring you to heare my Lord speake: pray ye goe,
there’s my key: if you do stirre abroad, goe arm’d.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Arm’d, Brother?

brother, I aduise you to the best, goe arm’d, I am no honest [C3]
man if there bee any good meaning towards you, I haue told
you what I haue seene & heard, but faintly, nothing
like the image and horror of it, pray you away?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Shall I heare from you anon?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
I doe serue you in this busines:Exit Edgar
A credulous Father, and a brother noble,
Whose nature is so farre from doing harmes,
That he suspects none, on whose foolish honesty
My practises ride easie, I see the busines,
Let me if not by birth, haue lands by wit,
All with me’s meete, that I can fashion fit.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Did my Father strike my gentleman for chi­
ding of his foole?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Yes Madam.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
By day and night he wrongs me,
Euery houre he flashes into one grosse crime or other
That sets vs all at ods, ile not indure it,
His Knights grow ryotous, and him selfe obrayds vs,
On euery trifell when he returnes from hunting,
I will not speake with him, say I am sicke,
If you come slacke of former seruices,
You shall doe well, the fault of it ile answere.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Hee’s coming Madam, I heare him.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Put on what wearie negligence you please,
you and your fellow seruants, i’de haue it come in question,
if he dislike it, let him to our sister,
whose mind and mine I know in that are one,
not to be ouerruld; idle old man that still would manage those
authorities that hee hath giuen away, now by my life old fooles
are babes again, & must be vs’d with checkes as flatteries, when
they are seene abusd, remember what I tell you.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Very well Madam.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
And let his Knights haue colder looks among
you, what growes of it no matter, aduise your fellowes
so, I would breed
from hence occasions, and I shall, that I may speake, ile write
straight to my sister to hould my very course, goe pre­
pare for dinner.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
If but as well I other accents borrow, [C3v]
that can my speech defuse, my good intent
may carry through it selfe to that full issue
for which I raz’d my likenes, now banisht Kent,
if thou canst serue where thou dost stand condem’d,
So may it come, thy maister whom thou louest
shall find the full of labour.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Let me not stay a iot for dinner, goe get it rea­
die, how now, what art thou?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: A man Sir.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
What dost thou professe? what would’st thou
with vs?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
I doe professe to be no lesse then I seeme, to serue
him truly that will put me in trust, to loue him that is
honest, to conuerse with him that is wise, and sayes little, to
feare iudgement, to fight when I cannot chuse, and to
eate no fishe.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What art thou?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
A very honest harted fellow, and as poore as
the king.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
If thou be as poore for a subiect, as he is for a
King, thar’t poore enough, what would’st thou?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Seruice.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Who would’st thou serue?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: You.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Do’st thou know me fellow?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
No sir, but you haue that in your countenance,
which I would faine call Maister.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Whats that?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Authoritie.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What seruices canst doe?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
I can keepe honest counsaile, ride, run, mar a
curious tale in telling it, and deliuer a plaine message
bluntly, that which ordinarie men are fit for, I am qual­
ified in, and the best of me, is diligence.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: How old art thou?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Not so yong to loue a woman for singing,
nor so old to dote on her for any thing, I haue yeares on
my backe fortie eight.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Follow mee, thou shalt serue mee, if I like thee no
worse after dinner, I will not part from thee yet, dinner,
ho dinner, wher’s my knaue, my foole, goe you and call
my foole hether, you sirra, whers my daughter?

sp.speaker: Steward.
sp.p: So please you,

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
What say’s the fellow there, call the clat­ [C4]
pole backe, whers my foole, ho I thinke the world’s
asleepe, how now, wher’s that mungrel?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: He say’s my Lord, your daughter is not well.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Why came not the slaue backe to mee when I
cal’d him?

sp.speaker: seruant.
sp.p:
Sir, hee answered mee in the roundest manner, hee
would not.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: A would not?

sp.speaker: seruant.
sp.p:
My Lord, I know not what the matter is,
but to my iudgemẽt, your highnes is not ẽtertained
with that ceremonious affection as you were wont,
ther’s a great abatement of kindnesse, apeer’s as well in
the generall dependants, as in the Duke himselfe also, and
your daughter.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Ha, say’st thou so?

sp.speaker: seruant.
sp.p:
I beseech you pardon mee my Lord, if I be
mistaken, for my dutie cannot bee silent, when I thinke
your highnesse wrong’d.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Thou but remember’st me of mine owne con­
ception, I haue perceiued a most faint neglect of late,
which I haue rather blamed as mine owne ielous curio­
sitie, then as a very pretence & purport of vnkindnesse,
I will looke further into’t, but wher’s this foole? I
haue not seene him this two dayes.

sp.speaker: seruant.
sp.p:
Since my yong Ladies going into France (qq4va)
sir, the foole hath much pined away.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
No more of that, I haue noted it, goe you
and tell my daughter, I would speake with her, goe you
cal hither my foole, O you sir, you sir, come you hither,
who am I sir?

sp.speaker: Steward.
sp.p: My Ladies Father.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
My Ladies father, my Lords knaue, you hore­
son dog, you slaue, you cur.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p:
I am none of this my Lord,
I beseech you pardon me.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Doe you bandie lookes with me you rascall?

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Ile not be struck my Lord,

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Nor tript neither, you base football player.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
I thanke thee fellow,
thou seru’st me, and ile loue thee.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Come sir arise, away, ile teach you differences,
away, away, if you will measure your lubbers, length a­
gaine tarry, but away, goe too, you haue wisedome, so.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Now friendly knaue I thanke thee, their’s
earnest of thy seruice.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Let me hire him too, heer’s my coxcombe.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: How now my prety knaue, how do’st thou?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Sirra, you were best take my coxcombe.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Why Foole?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Why for taking on’s part, that’s out of fauour,
nay and thou can’st not smile as the wind sits, thou’t catch
cold shortly, there take my coxcombe; why this fellow
hath banisht two on’s daughters, and done the third a
blessing against his will, if thou follow him, thou must
needs weare my coxcombe, how now nuncle, would
I had two coxcombes, and two daughters.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Why my boy?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
If I gaue them any liuing, id’e keepe my cox­
combs my selfe, ther’s mine, beg another of thy
daughters.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Take heede sirra, the whip.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Truth is a dog that must to kenell, hee must bee
whipt out, when Ladie oth’e brach may stand by the fire
and stincke.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: A pestilent gull to mee.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Sirra ile teach thee a speech.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Doe.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Marke it vncle,
haue more then thou shewest,
speake lesse then thou knowest,
lend lesse then thou owest,
ride more then thou goest,
learne more then thou trowest,
set lesse then thou throwest,
leaue thy drinke and thy whore,
and keepe in a doore,
and thou shalt haue more,
then two tens to a score.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: This is nothing foole.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Then like the breath of an vnfeed Lawyer,
you gaue me nothing for’t, can you make no vse of no­
thing vncle?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Why no boy,
nothing can be made out of nothing.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Prethee tell him so much the rent of his land
comes to, he will not beleeue a foole.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: A bitter foole.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Doo’st know the difference my boy, be­
tweene a bitter foole, and a sweete foole.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No lad, teach mee.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
That Lord that counsail’d thee to giue away thy land,
Come place him heere by mee, doe thou for him stand,
The sweet and bitter foole will presently appeare,
The one in motley here, the other found out there.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Do’st thou call mee foole boy?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
All thy other Titles thou hast giuen away, that thou
wast borne with.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: This is not altogether foole my Lord.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
No faith, Lords and great men will not let me, if I had
a monopolie out, they would haue part an’t, and lodes too, they
will not let me haue all the foole to my selfe, they’l be snatching;
giue me an egge Nuncle, and ile giue thee
two crownes.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What two crownes shall they be?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Why, after I haue cut the egge in the middle and
eate vp the meate, the two crownes of the egge; when
thou clouest thy crowne it’h middle, and gauest away
both parts, thou borest thy asse at’h backe or’e the
durt, thou had’st little wit in thy bald crowne, when thou
gauest thy golden one away, if I speake like my selfe in
this, let him be whipt that first finds it so.
Fooles had nere lesse wit in a yeare,
For wise men are growne foppish,
They know not how their wits doe weare,
Their manners are so apish.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: When were you wont to be so full of songs sirra?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
I haue vs’d it nuncle, euer since thou mad’st
thy daughters thy mother, for when thou gauest them
the rod, and put’st downe thine own breeches, then they
for sudden ioy did weep,
and I for sorrow sung,
that such a King should play bo-peepe,
and goe the fooles among:
prethe Nunckle keepe a schoolemaster that can teach
thy foole to lye, I would faine learne lye.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: And you lye, weele haue you whipt.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
I maruell what kin thou and thy daughters are,
they’l haue me whipt for speaking true, thou wilt haue mee
whipt for lying, and sometime I am whipt for holding
my peace, I had rather be any kind of thing then a foole,
and yet I would not bee thee Nuncle, thou hast pared thy
wit a both sides, & left nothing in the middle, here
comes one of the parings.

How now daughter, what makes that Frontlet on,
Me thinks you are too much alate it’h frowne.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Thou wast a prettie fellow when thou had’st no
need to care for her frowne, thou, thou art an O with­
out a figure, I am better then thou art now, I am a foole, [D1v]
thou art nothing, yes forsooth I will hould my tongue, so
your face bids mee, though you say nothing.
Mum, mum, he that keepes neither crust nor crum,
Wearie of all, shall want some. That’s a sheald pescod.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Not onely sir this, your all-licenc’d foole,
but other of your insolent retinue
do hourely carpe and quarrell, breaking forth
in ranke & (not to be indured riots,) Sir
I had thought by making this well knowne vnto you,
to haue found a safe redres, but now grow fearefull
by what your selfe too late haue spoke and done,
that you protect this course, and put on
by your allowance, which if you should, the fault
would not scape censure, nor the redresse, sleepe,
which in the tender of a wholsome weale,
might in their working doe you that offence,
that else were shame, that then necessitie
must call discreet proceedings.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
For you trow nuncle, the hedge sparrow
fed the Cookow so long, that it had it head bit off beit
young, so out went the candle, and we were left dark­
ling.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Are you our daughter?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Come sir, I would you would make vse of that good wisedome
whereof I know you are fraught, and put away
these dispositions, that of late transforme you
from what you rightly are.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
May not an Asse know when the cart drawes
the horse,
whoop Iug I loue thee.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Doth any here know mee?
why this is not Lear,
doth Lear walke thus? speake thus? where are his eyes,
either his notion, weaknes, or his discernings
are lethergie, sleeping, or wakeing; ha! sure tis not so,
who is it that can tell me who I am?
Lears shadow?
I would learne that, for by the markes of soueraintie,
knowledge, and reason, I should bee false perswaded I had
daughters.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Which they, will make an obedient father.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Your name faire gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Come sir, this admiration is much of the sauour
of other your new prankes, I doe beseech you
vnderstand my purposes aright,
as you are old and reuerend, should be wise,
here do you keepe a 100. Knights and Squires,
men so disordred, so deboyst and bold,
that this our court infected with their manners, [D2]
showes like a riotous Inne, epicurisme, and lust
make more like a tauerne or brothell,
then a great pallace, the shame it selfe doth speake
for instant remedie, be thou desired
by her, that else will take the thing shee begs,
a little to disquantitie your traine,
and the remainder that shall still depend,
to bee such men as may besort your age,
that know themselues and you.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Darkenes, and Deuils!
saddle my horses, call my traine together,
degenerate bastard, ile not trouble thee,
yet haue I left a daughter.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
You strike my people, and your disordred rabble,
make seruants of their betters.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
We that too late repent’s, O sir, are you come?
is it your will, speake Sir? that wee prepare any horses,
ingratitude! thou marble harted fiend,
more hideous when thou shewest thee in a child,
then the Sea-monster,

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.p: Pray Sir be patient.

detested kite, thou list
my traine, and men of choise and rarest parts,
that all particulars of dutie knowe,
and in the most exact regard, support
the worships of their name, O most small fault,
how vgly did’st thou in Cordelia shewe,
that like an engine wrencht my frame of nature
from the fixt place, drew from my heart all loue
and added to the gall, O Lear. Lear!
beat at this gate that let thy folly in,
and thy deere iudgement out, goe goe, my people?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
My Lord, I am giltles as I am ignorant.
Of what hath moued you.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
It may be so my Lord,
harke Nature, heare deere Goddesse, heare:
suspend thy purpose, if thou did’st intend
to make this creature fruitful
into her wombe, conuey sterility,
drie vp in hir the organs of increase,
and from her derogate body neuer spring
a babe to honour her, if shee must teeme,
create her childe of spleene, that it may liue
and bee a thourt disuetur’d torment to her,
let it stampe wrinckles in her brow of youth,
with accent teares, fret channels in her cheeks, (qq5b)
turne all her mothers paines and benefits
to laughter and contempt, that shee may feele, that she may feele,
how sharper then a serpents tooth it is,
to haue a thanklesse child, goe, goe, my people?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
Now Gods that we adore,
whereof comes this!

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Neuer afflict your selfe to know the cause,
but let his disposition haue that scope
that dotage giues it.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
What, fiftie of my followers at a clap,
within a fortnight?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What is the matter sir?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Ile tell thee,
life and death! I am asham’d
that thou hast power to shake my manhood thus,
that these hot teares that breake from me perforce,
should make the worst
blasts and fogs vpon the
vntender woundings of a fathers cursse,
peruse euery sence about the old fond eyes,
beweepe this cause againe, ile pluck you out,
& you cast with the waters that you make
to temper clay, yea, i’st come to this? Ha? Let it be so.
yet haue I left a daughter,
whom I am sure is kind and comfortable,
when shee shall heare this of thee, with her nailes
shee’l flea thy woluish visage, thou shalt find
that ile resume the shape, which thou dost thinke
I haue cast off for euer, thou shalt I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: Doe you marke that my Lord?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
I cannot bee so partiall Gonorill
to the great loue I beare you,

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Come sir no more,
you, more knaue then foole, after your master?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Nunckle Lear, Nunckle Lear,
tary and take the foole with
a fox when one has caught her,
and such a daughter
should sure to the slaughter,
if my cap would buy a halter,
so the foole followes after.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: What Oswald, ho.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
This man hath had good Counsell,
A hundred Knights?
’Tis politike, and safe to let him keepe
At point a hundred Knights: yes, that on euerie dreame,
Each buz, each fancie, each complaint, dislike,
He may enguard his dotage with their powres,
And hold our liues in mercy. Oswald, I say.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.p: Well, you may feare too farre.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Safer then trust too farre;
Let me still take away the harmes I feare,
Not feare still to be taken. I know his heart,
What he hath vtter’d I haue writ my Sister:
If she sustaine him, and his hundred Knights
When I haue shew’d th’vnfitnesse.
Enter Steward.
How now Oswald?

sp.speaker: Oswald.
sp.p: Here Madam.
What haue you writ this letter to my sister?

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.p: Yes Madam.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Take you some company, and away to horse,
informe her full of my particular feares,
and thereto add such reasons of your owne,
as may compact it more, get you gon, (qq5va)
and after your returne now my Lord,
this mildie gentlenes and course of yours
though I dislike not, yet vnder pardon
y’are much more alapt want of wisedome,
then praise for harmfull mildnes.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
How farre your eyes may pearce I cannot tell,
striuing to better ought, we marre whats well.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: Nay then.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Well, well, the euent,

div.head: Scena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Lear. Kent, Gentleman, and Foole.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Goe you before to Gloster with these letters,
acquaint my daughter no further with any thing you
know, then comes from her demand out of the letter,
if your diligence be not speedie, I shall be there before
you.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
I will not sleepe my Lord, till I haue deliuered
your letter.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
If a mans braines where in his heeles, wert not in
danger of kibes?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: I boy.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Then I prethe be mery, thy wit shal nere goe
slipshod.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Ha ha ha.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Shalt see thy other daughter will vse thee kind­
ly, for though shees as like this, as a crab is like an
apple, yet I con, what I can tel.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Why what canst thou tell my boy?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Sheel tast as like this, as a crab doth to a
crab, thou canst not tell why ones nose stande in the middle
of his face?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Why, to keep his eyes on either side’s nose,
that what a man cannot smell out, a may spie into.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: I did her wrong.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Canst tell how an Oyster makes his shell.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Nor I neither, but I can tell why a snayle has
a house.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Why, to put his head in, not to giue it away to his
daughter, and leaue his hornes without a case.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
I will forget my nature, so kind a father; be
my horses readie?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Thy Asses are gone about them, the reason why
the seuen starres are no more then seuen, is a prettie reason.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Because they are not eight.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Yes thou wouldst make a good foole.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: To tak’t againe perforce, Monster, ingratitude!

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p:
If thou wert my foole Nunckle, id’e haue thee
beatẽ for being old before thy time.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Hows that?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Thou shouldst not haue beene old, before thou hadst
beene wise.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
O let me not be mad sweet heauen! I would not be mad,
keepe me in temper, I would not be mad, How now are
the horses readie?

sp.speaker: Seruant.
sp.p: Readie my Lord.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Come boy.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Shee that is maide now, and laughs at my departure,
Shall not be a maide long, except things be cut shorter.

div.head: Actus Secundus. Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Saue thee Curan.

sp.speaker: Curan.
sp.p:
And you Sir, I haue beene
with your father, and giuen him notice,
that the Duke of Cornwall and his Dutches
will bee here with him to night.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: How comes that?

sp.speaker: Curan.
sp.p:
Nay, I know not, you haue heard of the newes a­
broad, I meane the whisperd ones, for there are yet but
eare-bussing arguments.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Not, I pray you what are they?

sp.speaker: Curan.
sp.p:
Haue you heard of no likely warres towards,
twixt the two Dukes of Cornwall and Albany?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Not a word.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
The Duke be here to night! the better best,
this weaues it selfe perforce into my busines,
my father hath set gard to take my brother,
and I haue one thing of a quesie question,
which must aske breefnes and fortune helpe;
Enter Edgar
brother, a word, discend brother I say,
my father watches, O flie this place,
intelligence is giuen where you are hid,
you haue now the good aduantage of the night,
haue you not spoken gainst the Duke of Cornwall ought,
hee’s coming hether now in the night, it’h hast,
and Regan with him, haue you nothing said
vpon his partie against the Duke of Albany,
aduise your— selfe.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: I am sure on’t not a word.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
I heare my father coming, pardon me
in crauing, I must draw my sword vpon you,
Draw, seeme to defend your selfe,
now quit you well,
yeeld, come before my father, light here, here,
flie brother flie, torches, torches, so farwell;
Exit Edgar.
some bloud drawne on mee would beget opinion
of my more fierce indeuour, I haue seene drunckards
doe more then this in sport, father, father,
stop, stop, no, helpe?

div.stage: Enter Glost. and Seruants with Torches.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Now Edmund where is the villaine?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
Here stood he in the darke, his sharpe sword out,
warbling of wicked charms, coniuring the Moone
to stand’s auspicious Mistris.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: But where is he?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Looke sir, I bleed.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Where is the villaine Edmund?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Fled this way sir, when by no meanes he could—

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Pursue him, go after, by no meanes, what?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
Perswade me to the murder of your Lordship, (qq6a)
but that I told him the reuengiue Gods,
gainst Paracides did all their thunders bend,
spoke with how many fould and strong a bond
the child was bound to the father, sir in a fine,
seeing how loathly opposite I stood,
to his vnnaturall purpose, with fell motion
with his prepared sword, hee charges home
my vnprouided body, lancht mine arme,
but when he saw my best alarumd spirits,
bould in the quarrels, rights, rousd to the encounter,
or whether gasted by the noyse I made,
but sodainly he fled.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
Let him flie farre,
not in this land shall hee remaine vncaught
and found, dispatch, the noble Duke my maister,
my worthy Arch and Patron, comes to night,
by his authoritie I will proclaime it,
that he which finds him shall deserue our thankes,
bringing the murderous caytife to the stake,
hee that conceals him, death.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p:
When I disswaded him from his intent,
and found him pight to doe it, with curst speech
I threatned to discouer him, he replyed,
thou vnpossessing Bastard, dost thou thinke,
if I would stand against thee, could the reposure
of any trust, vertue, or worth in thee
make thy words fayth’d? no. what I should denie,
as this I would, I, though thou didst produce
my very character, id’e turne it all
to thy suggestion, plot, and damned pretence,
and thou must make a dullard of the world,
if they not thought the profits of my death,
were very pregnant and potentiall spurres
to make thee seeke it.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
Strong and fastned villaine,
would he denie his letter, said he? I neuer got him,
harke the Dukes trumpets, I know not why he comes,
all Ports ile barre, the villaine shall not scape,
the Duke must grant mee that, besides, his picture
I will send farre and neere, that all the kingdome
may haue note of him, and of my land
loyall and naturall boy, ile worke the meanes
to make thee capable.

div.stage: Enter the Duke of Cornwall. Regan, and Attendants.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p:
How now my noble friend, since I came hether,
which I can call but now, I haue heard strange newes.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
If it be true, all vengeance comes too short [D4v]
which can pursue the offender, how dost my Lord?

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Madam my old heart is crackt, is crackt.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
What, did my fathers godson seeke your life?
he whom my father named your Edgar?

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: I Ladie, Ladie, shame would haue it hid.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
Was he not companion with the ryotous knights,
that tends vpon my father?

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: I know not Madam, tis too bad, too bad.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Yes Madam, he was of that consort.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
No maruaile then though he were ill affected,
Tis they haue put him on the old mans death,
To haue these—and wast of this his reuenues:
I haue this present euening from my sister,
Beene well inform’d of them, and with such cautions,
That if they come to soiourne at my house, ile not be there.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
Nor I, assure thee Regan; (qq6b)
Edmund, I heard that you haue shewen your father
a child-like office.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: Twas my dutie Sir.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
He did betray his practise, and receiued
This hurt you see, striuing to apprehend him.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Is he pursued?

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: I my good Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
If he be taken, he shall neuer more
be feard of doing harme, make your own purpose
how in my strength you please, for you Edmund,
whose vertue and obedience, doth this instant
so much commend it selfe, you shall bee ours,
natures of such deepe trust, wee shall much need
you, we first seaze on.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: I shall serue you truly, how euer else.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: For him I thanke your grace.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: You know not why we came to visit you?

sp.speaker: Regan.
sp.p:
Thus out of season, threatning darke ey’d night,
Ocasions noble Gloster of some prise,
Wherein we must haue vse of your aduise,
Our Father he hath writ, so hath our sister,
Of defences, which I best thought it fit,
To answer from our hand, the seuerall messengers
From hence attend dispatch, our good old friend,
Lay comforts to your bosome, & bestow your needfull councell
To our busines, which craues the instant vse.

div.head: Scena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Steward.
sp.p: Good deuen to thee friend, art of the house?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Where may we set our horses?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: It’h mire.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Prethee if thou loue me, tell me.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I loue thee not.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Why then I care not for thee.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
If I had thee in Lipsburie pinfold, I would make
thee care for mee.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Why dost thou vse me thus? I know thee not.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Fellow I know thee.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: What dost thou know me for?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
A knaue, a rascall, an eater of broken meates, a
base, proud, shallow, beggerly, three snyted hundred
pound, filthy wosted stocken knaue, a lilly lyuer’d
action taking knaue, a whorson glassegazing super­
finicall rogue, one truncke inheriting slaue, one that
would’st bee a baud in way of good seruice, and art no­
thing but the composition of a knaue, begger, coward,
pander, and the sonne and heire of a mungrell bitch,
whom I will beat into clamarous whyning, if thou
denie the least sillable of the addition.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p:
What a monstrous fellow art thou, thus
to raile on one, that’s neither knowne of thee, nor
knowes thee.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
What a brazen fac’t varlet art thou, to deny
thou knowest mee, is it two dayes agoe since I beat thee, and tript vp thy
heeles before the King? draw you rogue, (qq6va)
for though it be night the Moone shines, ile make a
sop of the moone-shine a’you, draw you whorson cullyonly
barber-munger, draw?

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Away, I haue nothing to doe with thee.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Draw you rascall, you bring letters a­
gainst the King, and take Vanitie the puppets part, a­
gainst the royaltie of her father, draw you rogue or
ile so carbonado your shankes, draw you rascall, come
your wayes.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Helpe, ho, murther, helpe.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Strike you slaue, stand rogue, stand you neate
slaue, strike.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Helpe, ho, murther, helpe.

div.stage: Enter Edmund with his rapier drawne, Gloster the Duke and Dutchesse.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: How now, whats the matter? Part.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
With you goodman boy, and you please come,
ile fleash you, come on yong maister.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Weapons, armes, whats the matter here?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
Keepe peace vpon your liues, hee dies that strikes
againe, what’s the matter?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: The messengers from our sister, and the King.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Whats your difference, speake?

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: I am scarse in breath my Lord.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
No maruaile you haue so bestir’d your valour,
you cowardly rascall, nature disclaimes in thee, a Tayler
made thee.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Thou art a strange fellow, a Taylor make a man.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
I, a Tayler sir; a Stone-cutter, or a Painter could
not haue made him so ill, though hee had beene but two
houres at the trade.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: Speake yet, how grew your quarrell?

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p:
This ancient ruffen sir, whose life I haue spar’d
at sute of his gray-beard.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Thou whorson Zedd, thou vnnecessarie letter,
my Lord if you’l giue mee leaue, I will tread this vn­
boulted villaine into morter, and daube the walles of a
iaques with him, spare my gray beard you wagtayle.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
Peace sir,
you beastly Knaue you haue no reuerence.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Yes sir, but anger has a priuiledge.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Why art thou angry?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
That such a slaue as this should weare a sword,
That weares no honesty, such smiling roges as these,
Like Rats oft bite those cordes in twaine,
Which are to intrench, to inloose smooth euery passion
That in the natures of their Lords rebell,
Bring oyle to stir, snow to their colder-moods,
Reneag, affirme, and turne their halcion beakes
With euery gale and varie of their maisters,
Knowing nought like dayes but following, a plague vpon your epeliptick
Visage, smoyle you my speeches, as I were a foole?
Goose and I had you vpon Sarum plaine,
Id’e send you cackling home to Camulet.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What art thou mad old fellow?

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: How fell you out, say that?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
No contraries hold more, antipathy,
Then I and such a knaue.

p.nvsSeg: Why dost thou call him knaue,

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: His countenance likes me not.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: No more perchance does mine, or his, or hers.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Sir tis my occupation to be plaine,
I haue seene better faces in my time (qq6vb)
That stands on any shoulder that I see
Before me at this instant.

p.nvsSeg: these kind of knaues I know

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Sir in good sooth, or in sincere veritie,
Vnder the allowance of your graund aspect,
Whose influence like the wreath of radient fire
In flitkering Phœbus front.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What mean’st thou by this?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
To goe out of my dialogue which you discom­
mend so much, I know sir, I am no flatterer, he that be­
guild you in a plain accent, was a plaine knaue, which
for my part I will not bee, though I should win your
displeasure, to intreat mee too’t.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What’s the offence you gaue him?

I neuer gaue him any, it pleas’d the King his maister
Very late to strike at me vpon his misconstruction,
When he coniunct and flattering his displeasure
Tript me behind, being downe, insulted, rayld,
And put vpon him such a deale of man, that,
That worthied him, got prayses of the King,
For him attempting who was selfe subdued,
And in the flechuent of this dread exploit,
Drew on me here againe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
Bring forth the stockes ho?
You stubburne ausrent knaue, you reuerent bragart,
Weele teach you.

I am too old to learne, call not your stockes for me,
I serue the King, on whose imployments I was sent to you,
You should doe small respect, shew too bold malice
Against the Grace and person of my maister,
Stobing his messenger.

Fetch forth the stockes? as I haue life and honour,
There shall he set till noone.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: Till noone, till night my Lord, and all night too.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Why Madam, if I were your fathers dogge,
you could not vse me so.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: Sir being his knaue, I will.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
This is a fellow of the selfe same nature,
Our sister speake of, come bring away the stockes?

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
Let me beseech your Grace not to doe so,
His fault is much, and the good King his maister
VVill check him for’t, your purpost low correction,
Is such, as belest and contaned wretches for pilfrings
And most common trespasses are punisht with,
The King must take it ill, that hee’s so slightly valued
In his messenger, should haue him thus restrained.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Ile answer that.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
My sister may receiue it much more worse,
To haue her Gentlemen abus’d, assalted
For following her affaires, put in his legges,
Come my good Lord away?

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
I am sory for thee friend, tis the Dukes pleasure,
VVhose disposition all the world well knowes
VVill not be rubd nor stopt, ile intreat for thee.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Pray you doe not sir, I haue watcht and trauaild hard,
Sometime I shal sleepe ont, the rest ile whistle,
A good mans fortune may grow out at heeles, (rr1a)
Giue you good morrow.

p.nvsSeg: The Dukes to blame in this,

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Good King that must approue the cõmon say,
Thou out of heauens benediction comest [E3]
To the warme Sunne.
Approach thou beacon to this vnder gloabe,
That by thy comfortable beames I may
Peruse this letter, nothing almost sees my rackles
But miserie, I know tis from Cordelia,
VVho hath not fortunately beene informed
Of my obscured course, and shall find time
From this enormious state, seeking to giue
Losses and remedies, all wearie and ouerwatch
Late vantage heauie eyes not to behold
This shamefull lodging, Fortune goodnight,
Smile, once more turne thy wheele.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p:
I heare my selfe proclaim’d,
And by the happie hollow of a tree
Escapt the hunt, no Port is free, no place
That guard, and most vnusuall vigilence
Dost not attend my taking while I may scape,
I will preserue my selfe, and am bethought
To take the basest and most poorest shape,
That euer penury in contempt of man,
Brought neare to beast, my face ile grime with filth,
Blanket my loynes, else all my haire with knots,
And with presented nakednes outface,
The wind, and persecution of the skie,
The Countrie giues me proofe and president
Of Bedlam beggers, who with roring voyces,
Strike in their numb’d mortified bare armes,
Pies, wodden prickes, nayles, sprigs of rosemary,
And with this horrible obiect frame low seruice,
Poore pelting villages, sheep-coates, and milles,
Sometime with lunaticke bans, sometime with prayers
Enforce their charitie, poore Tuelygod, poore Tom,
That’s something yet, Edgar I nothing am.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Tis strange that they should so depart from hence,
And not send backe my messenger.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Hayle to thee noble maister.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: How, mak’st thou this shame thy pastime?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: No my Lord.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Ha ha, looke he weares crewell garters,
Horses are tide by the heeles, dogges and beares
Byt’h necke, munkies bit’h loynes, and men
Byt’h legges, when a mans ouer lusty at legs,
Then he weares wooden neatherstockes.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Whats he,
that hath so much thy place mistooke
to set thee here?

p.nvsSeg: It is both he and shee,

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No I say,

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I say yea.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No no, they would not.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Yes they haue.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: By Iupiter I sweare no,

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: By Iuno, I sweare I.

they durst not do’t,
They would not, could not do’t, tis worse then murder,
To doe vpon respect such violent outrage,
Resolue me with all modest hast, which way
Thou may’st deserue, or they purpose this vsage,
Coming from vs.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
My Lord, when at their home
I did commend your highnes letters to them,
Ere I was risen from the place that shewed
My dutie kneeling, came there a reeking Post,
Stewd in his hast, halfe breathles, panting forth
From Gonorill his mistris, salutations,
Deliuered letters spite of intermission,
Which presently they read, on whose contents
They summond vp their men, straight tooke horse,
Commanded me to follow, and attend the leasure
Of their answere, gaue me cold lookes,
And meeting here the other messenger,
Whose welcome I perceau’d had poyson’d mine,
Being the very fellow that of late
Display’d so sawcily against your Highnes,
Hauing more man then wit about me drew,
He raised the house with loud and coward cries,
Your sonne and daughter found this trespas worth [E4]
This shame which here it suffers.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Winters not gon yet, if the wil’d Geese fly that way,
Fathers that weare rags, do make their Children blind,
But Fathers that beare bags, shall see their children kind.
Fortune that arrant whore, nere turns the key toth’ poore.
But for all this thou shalt haue as many Dolors for thy
Daughters, as thou canst tell in a yeare.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
O how this mother swels vp toward my hart,
Historica passio downe thou climing sorrow,
Thy element’s below, where is this daughter?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: With the Earle sir within,

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Follow me not, stay there?

sp.speaker: Knight.
sp.p:
Made you no more offẽce
then what you speake of?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
No,
how chance the King comes with so small a traine?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
And thou hadst beene set in the stockes for that
question, thou ha’dst well deserued it.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Why foole?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Weele set thee to schoole to an Ant, to teach
thee ther’s no labouring in the winter, all that follow their
noses, are led by their eyes, but blind men, and ther’s
not a nose among a 100. but can smell him thats stinck­
ing, let goe thy hold when a great wheele runs downe a
hill, least it breake thy necke with following it, but the
great one that goes vp the hill, let him draw thee after,
when a wise man giues thee better councell, giue mee mine
againe, I would haue none but knaues follow it, since a
foole giues it.
That Sir that serues and seekes for gaine,
And followes but for forme:
Will packe when it begin to raine,
And leaue thee in the storme.
But I will tarie, the foole will stay,
And let the wise man flie:
The knaue turnes foole that runs away,
The foole no knaue perdy.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Where learnt you this foole?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Not in the stockes.

Denie to speake with mee, th’are sicke, th’are weary,
They traueled hard to night, meare Iustice,
I the Images of reuolt and flying off,
Fetch mee a better answere.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p:
My deere Lord,
you know the fierie qualitie of the Duke,
how vnremoueable and fixt he is
in his owne Course.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Vengeance, death, plague, confusion, [E4v]
what fierie quality, why Gloster, Gloster,
id’e speake with the Duke of Cornewall, and his wife.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: Well my good Lord, I haue inform’d them so.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Inform’d them? Do’st thou vnderstand me man.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: I my good Lord.

The King would speake with Cornewal, the deare fate
Would with the daughter speake, come and tends seruise,
Are they inform’d of this? My breath and blood:
The fierie Duke, tell the hot Duke that Lear,
Mo but not yet, may be he is not well,
Infirmitie doth still neglect all office, where to our health
Is boũd, we are not our selues, when nature being oprest
Cõmand the mind to suffer with the bodie, ile forbeare,
And am fallen out with my more hedier will,
To take the indispos’d and sickly fit, for the sound man,
Death on my state, wherfore should he sit here?
This act perswades me, that this remotion of the Duke & her
Is practise, only giue me my seruant forth,
Tell the Duke and’s wife, Ile speake with them
Now presently, bid them come forth and heare me,
Or at their chamber doore ile beat the drum,
Till it cry sleepe to death.

sp.speaker: Glost.
sp.p: I would haue all well betwixt you.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: O me my heart, my rising heart. But downe.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Cry to it Nunckle, as the Coknay did to the
eeles, when she put vm it’h past aliue, she rapt vm
ath coxcombs with a stick, and cryed downe wantons
downe, twas her brother, that in pure kindnes to his
horse buttered his hay.

div.stage: Enter Duke and Regan. Gloster, Seruants.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Good morrow to you both.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Hayle to your Grace.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: I am glad to see your highnes.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Regan I thinke you are, I know what reason
I haue to thinke so, if thou shouldst not be glad,
I would deuose me from thy mothers fruit,
Sepulchring an adultresse, yea are you free?
Some other time for that. Beloued Regan,
Thy sister is naught, oh Regan she hath tyed,
Sharpe tooth’d vnkindnes, like a vulture heare,
I can scarce speake to thee, thout not beleeue,
Of how deptoued a qualitie, O Regan.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
I pray sir take patience, I haue hope
You lesse know how to value her desert,
Then she to slacke her dutie.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Say? How is that?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
I cannot thinke my Sister in the least
Would faile her Obligation. If Sir perchance
She haue restrained the Riots of your Followres,
’Tis on such ground, and to such wholesome end,
As cleeres her from all blame.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: My cursses on her.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
O Sir you are old, (rr1vb)
Nature on you standes on the very verge of her confine,
You should be rul’d and led by some discretion,
That discernes your state better thẽ you your selfe,
Therfore I pray that to our sister, you do make returne,
Say you haue wrong’d her Sir?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Aske her forgiuenes,
Doe you marke how this becomes the house,
Deare daughter, I confesse that I am old,
Age is vnnecessarie, on my knees I beg,
That you’l vouchsafe me rayment, bed and food.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
Good sir no more, these are vnsightly tricks,
Returne you to my sister.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
No Regan,
She hath abated me of halfe my traine,
Lookt blacke vpon me, strooke mee with her tongue
Most Serpent-like vpon the very heart,
All the stor’d vengeances of heauen fall on her ingratful top,
Strike her yong bones, you taking ayrs with lamenes.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
Fie fie sir.
You nimble lightnings dart your blinding flames,
Into her scornfull eyes, infect her beautie,
You Fen suckt fogs, drawne by the powrefull Sunne,
To fall and blast her pride.

O the blest Gods, so will you wish on me,
When the rash mood—

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
No Regan, thou shalt neuer haue my curse,
The tẽder hested nature shall not giue the or’e
To harshnes, her eies are fierce, but thine do cõfort & not burne
Tis not in thee to grudge my pleasures, to cut off my traine,
To bandy hasty words, to scant my sizes,
And in conclusion, to oppose the bolt
Against my coming in, thou better knowest,
The offices of nature, bond of child-hood, [F1v]
Effects of curtesie, dues of gratitude,
Thy halfe of the kingdome, hast thou not forgot
Wherein I thee indow’d.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: Good sir too’th purpose.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Who put my man i’th stockes?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What trumpets that?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
I know’t my sisters, this approues her letters,
That she would soone be here, is your Lady come?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
This is a slaue, whose easie borrowed pride
Dwels in the fickle grace of her a followes,
Out varlot, from my sight.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What meanes your Grace?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Who struck my seruant, Regan I haue good hope
Thou didst not know ant.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Who comes here? O heauens!
If you doe loue old men, if you sweet sway alow
Obedience, if your selues are old, make it your cause,
Send downe and take my part,
Art not asham’d to looke vpon this beard?
O Regan wilt thou take her by the hand?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Why not by the hand sir, how haue I offended?
Als not offence that indiscretion finds,
And dotage tearmes so.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
O sides you are too tough,
Will you yet hold? how came my man it’h stockes?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
I set him there sir, but his owne disorders (rr2a)
Deseru’d much lesse aduancement,

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: You, did you?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
I pray you father being weake seeme so,
If till the expiration of your moneth,
You will returne and soiorne with my sister,
Dismissing halfe your traine, come then to me,
I am now from home, and out of that prouision,
Which shall be needful for your entertainment.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Returne to her, and fiftie men dismist,
No rather I abiure all roofes, and chuse
To wage against the enmitie of the Ayre,
To be a Comrade with the Woolfe and owle, [F2]
Necessities sharpe pinch, returne with her,
Why the hot bloud in France, that dowerles
Tooke our yongest borne, I could as well be brought
To knee his throne, and Squire-like pension bag,
To keepe base life afoot, returne with her,
Perswade me rather to be slaue and sumter
To this detested groome.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: At your choise sir.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Now I prithee daughter do not make me mad,
I will not trouble thee my child, farewell,
Wee’le no more meete, no more see one another.
But yet thou art my flesh, my bloud, my daughter,
Or rather a disease that lies within my flesh,
Which I must needs call mine, thou art a bile,
A plague sore, an imbossed carbuncle in my
Corrupted bloud, but Ile not chide thee,
Let shame come when it will, I doe not call it,
I doe not bid the thunder bearer shoote,
Nor tell tailes of thee to high Iudging Ioue,
Mend when thou canst, be better at thy leasure,
I can be patient, I can stay with Regan,
I and my hundred Knights.

Not altogether so sir, I looke not for you yet,
Nor am prouided for your fit welcome,
Giue eare sir to my sister, for those
That mingle reason with your passion,
Must be content to thinke you are old, and so,
But she knowes what shee does.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Is this well spoken now?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
I dare auouch it sir, what fiftie followers,
Is it not well, what should you need of more,
Yea or so many, sith that both charge and danger
Speakes gainst so great a number, how in a house
Should many people vnder two commands
Hold amytie, tis hard, almost impossible.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Why might not you my Lord receiue attendãce
From those that she cals seruants, or from mine?

Why not my Lord? if then they chanc’st to slacke you,
We could controwle them, if you will come to me, [F2v]
For now I spie a danger, I intreat you,
To bring but fiue and twentie, to no more
Will I giue place or notice.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: I gaue you all.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: And in good time you gaue it.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Made you my guardians, my depositaries,
But kept a reseruation to be followed
With such a number, what, must I come to you
With fiue and twentie, Regan said you so?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: And speak’t againe my Lord, no more with me.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.p:
Those wicked creatures yet do seem wel fauor’d
When others are more wicked, not being the worst
Stands in some ranke of prayse, Ile goe with thee,
Thy fifty yet doth double fiue and twentie,
And thou art twice her loue.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Heare me my Lord,
What need you fiue and twentie, tenne, or fiue,
To follow in a house, where twise so many
Haue a commaund to tend you.

sp.speaker: Regan.
sp.p: What needes one?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
O reason not the deed, our basest beggers,
Are in the poorest thing superfluous,
Allow not nature more then nature needes,
Mans life as cheape as beasts, thou art a Lady,
If onely to goe warme were gorgeous,
Why nature needes not, what thou gorgeous wearest
Which scarcely keepes thee warme, but for true need,
You heauens giue me that patience, patience I need,
You see me here (you Gods) a poore old fellow,
As full of greefe as age, wretched in both,
If it be you that stirres these daughters hearts
Against their Father, foole me not to much,
To beare it lamely, touch me with noble anger,
O let not womens weapons, water drops
Stayne my mans cheekes, no you vnnaturall hags,
I will haue such reuenges on you both,
That all the world shall, I will doe such things,
What they are yet I know not, but they shalbe [F3]
The terrors of the earth, you thinke ile weepe,
No ile not weepe, I haue full cause of weeping,
Storme and Tempest.
But this heart shall breake, in a 100. thousand flowes
Or ere ile weepe, O foole I shall goe mad.

div.stage: Exeunt Lear, Leister, Kent, and Foole.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Let vs withdraw, twill be a storme.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
This house is little the old man and his people,
Cannot be well bestowed.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Tis his own blame hath put himselfe from rest,
And must needs tast his folly.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
For his particuler, ile receiue him gladly,
But not one follower.

p.nvsSeg: where is my Lord of Gloster?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: Followed the old man forth, he is return’d.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: The King is in high rage,

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p: Whether is he going?
He cals to Horse, & wil I know not whether.

sp.speaker: Re.
sp.p: Tis good to giue him way, he leads himselfe.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: My Lord, intreat him by no meanes to stay.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p:
Alack the night comes on, and the bleak winds
Do sorely russel, for many miles about ther’s not a bush.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
O sir, to wilfull men
The iniuries that they themselues procure,
Must be their schoolemasters, shut vp your doores,
He is attended with a desperate traine,
And what they may incense him to, being apt,
To haue his eare abusd, wisedome bids feare.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
Shut vp your doores my Lord, tis a wild night,
My Reg counsails well, come out at’h storme.

div.head: Actus Tertius. Scena Prima.
div.stage: Storme still. Enter Kent and a Gentleman at seuerall doores.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Whats here beside foule weather?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: One minded like the weather most vnquietly.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I know you, whers the King?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p:
Contending with the fretfull element,
Bids the wind blow the earth into the sea,
Or swell the curled waters boue the maine
That things might change or cease, teares his white haire,
Which the impetuous blasts with eyles rage
Catch in their furie, and make nothing of,
Striues in his little world of man to outscorne, [F3v]
The too and fro conflicting wind and raine,
This night wherin the cub-drawne Beare would couch,
The Lyon, and the belly pinched Wolfe
Keepe their furre dry, vnbonneted he runnes,
And bids what will take all.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: But who is with him?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p:
None but the foole, who labours to out-iest
His heart strooke iniuries.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Sir I doe know you,
And dare vpon the warrant of my Arte,
Commend a deare thing to you, there is diuision,
Although as yet the face of it be couer’d,
With mutuall cunning, twixt Albany and Cornwall
Who haue, as who haue not, that their great Starres
Thron’d and set high; Seruants, who seeme no lesse,
Which are to France the Spies and Speculations
Intelligent of our State. What hath bin seene,
Either in snuffes, and packings of the Dukes,
Or the hard Reine which both of them hath borne
Against the old kinde King; or something deeper,
Whereof (perchance) these are but furnishings.
But true it is, from France there comes a power
Into this scattered kingdome, who alreadie wise in our negligẽce,
Haue secret feet in some of our best Ports,
And are at point to shew their open banner,
Now to you, if on my credit you dare build so farre,
To make your speed to Douer, you shall find
Some that will thanke you, making iust report
Of how vnnaturall and bemadding sorrow
The King hath cause to plaine,
I am a Gentleman of blood and breeding,
And from some knowledge and assurance,
Offer this office to you.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: I will talke farther with you.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
No doe not,
For confirmation that I much more
Then my outwall, open this purse and take
VVhat it containes, if you shall see Cordelia,
As feare not but you shall, shew her this ring,
And she will tell you who your fellow is,
That yet you doe not know, fie on this storme,
I will goe seeke the King.

p.nvsSeg: haue you no more to say?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Few words but to effect more then all yet:
That when we haue found the King, in which your pain
Ile this way, you that, he that first lights [F4]
On him, hollow the other.

div.head: Scena Secunda.
div.stage: Storme still. Enter Lear and Foole.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Blow wind & cracke your cheekes, rage, blow
You caterickes, & Hircanios spout til you haue drencht,
The steeples drown’d the cockes, you sulpherous and
Thought executing fires, vaunt-currers to
Oke-cleauing thunderboults, singe my white head,
And thou all shaking thunder, smite flat
The thicke Rotunditie of the world, cracke natures
Mold, all Germains spill at once that make
Ingratefull man.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
O Nunckle, Court holly water in a drie house
Is better then this raine water out a doore,
Good Nunckle in, and aske thy daughters blessing,
Heers a night pities nether wise man nor foole.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Rumble thy belly full, spit fire, spout raine,
Nor raine, wind, thunder, fire, are my daughters,
I taske not you you elements with vnkindnes,
I neuer gaue you kingdome, cald you children,
You owe me no subscription, why then let fall your horrible plesure
Here I stãd your slaue, a poore infirme weak &
Despis’d ould man, but yet I call you seruile
Ministers, that haue with 2. pernitious daughters ioin’d
Your high engẽdred battel gainst a head so old & white (rr2vb)
As this, O tis foule.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p:
Hee that has a house to put his head in, has a good
headpeece,
the Codpeece that will house before the head, has any
the head and hee shall lowse, so beggers mary many,
the man that makes his toe, what hee his heart should make,
shall haue a corne cry woe, and turne his sleepe to wake,
for there was neuer yet faire woman but shee made
mouthes in a glasse.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
No I will be the patterne of all patience
I will say nothing.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Whose there?
